title: Thoughts on Caligula: Ultimate Cut and yet more squandered artistic intentions

commenti.body:
I haven't seen the new cut, and don't know if I ever will, but I agree with your general assessment that this is also a compromised version because it has no clear reason for being.

Based on what I've gleaned from the three episodes of The Projection Booth podcast about Caligula, two of which interview Peter Tuschinski, Tuschinski's version of the project (which would have seen him team up with Tinto Brass to restore his cut based on a workprint and the film materials that Tuschinski located right before they were about to be destroyed) was cancelled when the head of Penthouse changed.

Negovan was a nepotism hire, an *utterly* unqualified individual who was given the job simply because he was friends with someone at Penthouse. He heard about Tuschinski and essentially extended him an offer of "give me all of your research for free to help me with my own version", which Tuschinski declined. At that point, Brass refused to even speak to Negovan.

This is the part that pisses me off: clearly Negovan was the wrong guy for the project and Brass wanted nothing to do with him. They already had the perfect person for the project, a filmmaker and Brass scholar who had befriended Brass (Tuschinski). The only reason this version didn't happen was because Negovan had been offered the job and wouldn't cede authority to Tuschinski or Brass. He acts like he wanted this, but that's obviously a lie because he spoke to Tuschinski and could have made it happen. Instead, he wanted Tuschinski's research and nothing else.

According to Negovan, once it was clear Brass wouldn't be involved, doing the Brass version was off the table because Brass's style was impossible to imitate (something Tuschinski would have rectified) and because... Negovan doesn't seem to respect Brass as a filmmaker. He doesn't even like Caligula as a movie. It's mind-boggling that Negovan was even involved in the first place... until you hear him talk about the film. Or, more correctly, talk about *himself and the book he is writing and the documentaries he's making* and all of the other tie-in stuff he's doing. He's clinging to Caligula to make himself relevant while talking smack about the movie and its director. Unbelievable.

It was originally announced as a restoration of Gore Vidal's vision, which shows you how little research they had done by that point (Vidal's script had been changed by Brass and McDowell before filming began). When that proved to be impossible, they proceeded to the next idea: just doing their own version. Negovan tries to sell this as "I just want the cast's performances to finally get their due", but that's an incredibly vague artistic intention. He also did things like add CGI backgrounds, a new animated prologue, and an entirely new score.

None of this makes sense as a "restoration".

There is really no other way of looking at this: it's another Penthouse cut. Or, perhaps even worse, it's an official Penthouse release of a Penthouse executive's friend's fan edit, that was made by giving said "fan" access to materials that even the director and his scholars weren't given access to.

To add insult to injury, the way Negovan talks about the "lost" footage doesn't give any credit to Tuschinski. He goes out of his way never to mention Tuschinski, without whom this new version would be impossible because all of the original film and audio materials would have been destroyed.

The more I heard about this project, the more disgusted I am by it. I have no respect for that Thomas Negovan did. It's a hatchet job with no clear reason to exist except that it allows him to insert himself into the history of a famous movie. I'm glad there's a "better" version of the movie, but it never should have existed in the first place and, worst, it probably prevented the creation of what people have been demanding for over forty years: the actual completion of the film by its original director, Tinto Brass.

I listened to those podcasts too. Heartbreaking to hear Tuschinski's descriptions of these scenes that sound so interesting, that we will probably never see while Penthouse are intent on undoing what goodwill there was in restoring Caligula.

>Negovan was a nepotism hire, an utterly unqualified individual who was given the job simply because he was friends with someone at Penthouse.

This actually fills in a lot of those details I puzzled over with the approach taken, and also why Tuschinski won't speculate on why it was he mysteriously got canned the minute leadership changed. Obviously this was the new Penthouse guy killing a legacy project from the previous boss, or rather putting in someone that would be "their own". Fucking sad beyond words, and now I feel bad for owning the set...although I am glad for Io, Caligola, the Italian version I'll have to sit down and properly watch. Perhaps it will be the only saving grace in this shitshow, that there is a version hidden on disc 4 of the set showcasing a skeleton of what could've been.

I admire your expertise on this matter, and all your criticisms sound reasonable but I have to say that I saw the Ultimate cut in theaters as a *Caligula* newb (never seen any versions) and loved it. I was just in awe of the splendor of it all, and save for a few moments where it dragged, I found the narrative quite compelling. I knew that what I was getting was by no means a reconstruction of the original authorial intent, but I find the idea of a fan-made reconstruction using previously unseen takes quite interesting conceptually. I enjoyed the music, and found the edit to actually be quite heavy on the wide-shots. Again, this is before I compare to previous versions, but I didn't really notice the overuse of medium shots you describe.

I don't know what the rights issues were that prevented this from being recut as Tinto Brass intended, but I can only hope that this drums up enough interest for that. If anything else, it got people like me and some friends into the theater to appreciate a truly unique piece of art.

There are no rights issues, Penthouse owns the footage. They were on board with Tinto and his scholar collaborating until leadership changed.

I'm glad you enjoyed the film, as far as the prformances go this one is certainly showcasing the best of Malcolm McDowell and Helen Mirren, as well as other actors.

Undoubtedly not having seen the other, vastly vastly different cuts, that will colour opinion. For me, knowing the history and having seen elements of the original intent, it's a tough thing to watch. While it's up to you whether watching the botched theatrical uncut is worth your time, you will be able to see certainly in every other cut, the style and the intention for those sets, is quite different. There are plenty more wide shots in the original versions, not only for all the splendour but also to get in the nudity, which Negovan for some reason chose to cut. It's not by any means shaving corners on Michaelangelo's David (the film will never be that good), but it is going against artistic intention not to follow the style of what was shot. Tinto Brass and in particular Donito Donali, the set designer, intended much different. Frankly it is an insult for Negovan to CGI in things on top of Donali's designs, being Donali would go on to win an Oscar for set design in Fellini's Casanova for similar styles and techniques. His sets are meant to look stagey as they are about real-looking grandness.

Yeah, remember that comment in the latest TPB episode where Tuschinski refers to a rumor he heard about the materials being mishandled? That they had to be careful about opening the cans because the contents might just disintegrate, implying that they destroyed some footage through sheer incompetence?

This absolutely is just Penthouse cashing in on the demand for a director's cut by doubling down on their original crime of recutting the film. I'm really curious to hear how scholars address this in the future. At best, it will be regarded as a curiosity but a missed opportunity. At worst, this is even worse than what they did forty years ago, because they are cynically cashing in on the original crime by doing it again.

Well having read and watched some of that, it's a shame they railroaded Tuschinski, I wish the new version didn't come at his and Brass's expense. Nevertheless, as a standalone film, I do think the "Ultimate" cut is pretty great.

Like I said I'm glad you enjoyed the cut. I actually wish I could've felt the same!

If you're interested to know what Tinto's style when given the freedom is, I recommend Salon Kitty, his prior film about a Nazi operated brothel that doubled as an intelligence gathering operation for Himmler. Truth be told his style for me is clumsy by today's standards, though yeah I'm just a big proponent of auteur theory and creative freedom which is why I desperately want his cut for Caligula.

I watched the Ultimate Cut for the first time a few days ago. It very clearly still has a lot of nudity in it and there's stills some full-blown sex going on in the background. 

I think it's definitely the best version of the film, especially for the acting side. It's amazing to finally hear all of the original audio from the actors, especially all of the actors who were dubbed.

I recommend watching Salon Kitty if you're not sure what I mean. My post isn't really about nudity or no nudity, it's about the director's very distinct style being almost surgically removed in the latest cut.
